title: Remote Learning
description: A news report, a teacher and a parent discussing online classes, a student interview and a lecture on how to learn well at home.
instructions: Read the questions for each part first. Then press Play and listen. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part 1 · Radio news report
parts.intro: You will hear a radio reporter talking about online schooling.

script.speaker: Reporter
script.text: Good morning. A new report published this week has looked at how remote learning has changed education over the last few years, and the results are more mixed than many people expected.

script.speaker: Reporter
script.text: When schools first closed, millions of children suddenly had to study from home. Some families had a quiet room and a fast connection, but others shared one old laptop between three children, and this gap in equipment mattered a great deal.

script.speaker: Reporter
script.text: The researchers found that younger children generally lost the most. Without a teacher in the room, they found it difficult to concentrate, and many fell several months behind in reading.

script.speaker: Reporter
script.text: Older students, however, often did better than expected. Many said they liked being able to work at their own speed, and some even felt less anxious without the pressure of a crowded classroom.

script.speaker: Reporter
script.text: Interestingly, the report doesn't say that online learning is bad. It says that it works best when it is combined with face-to-face contact, with regular live lessons rather than recorded videos alone.

script.speaker: Reporter
script.text: The authors also stress that teachers need training. Using a video platform is easy, but designing an interesting online lesson is a skill that takes time, and many teachers had to learn it overnight.

parts.title: Part 2 · A teacher and a parent
parts.intro: You will hear a teacher, Ms Parker, talking to a parent, Mr Nguyen, at a school meeting.

script.speaker: Nguyen
script.text: Thank you for seeing me, Ms Parker. I wanted to talk about my son, Minh. He's been doing his lessons online two days a week, and I'm not sure it's working.

script.speaker: Parker
script.text: I'm glad you came. What worries you most?

script.speaker: Nguyen
script.text: Well, he says he's fine, but whenever I walk past his room, he seems to be watching videos or chatting with friends, not studying.

script.speaker: Parker
script.text: That's very common, I'm afraid. It's hard for any teenager to resist distractions when the phone is next to the keyboard. But I should say that Minh's results are actually good. His last essay was one of the best in the class.

script.speaker: Nguyen
script.text: Really? That's a relief. Then why do I feel uneasy?

script.speaker: Parker
script.text: Perhaps because you can't see him working. In the classroom you would see him with a pen in his hand, and you'd know he was busy. At home it looks like nothing, even when the thinking is happening.

script.speaker: Nguyen
script.text: I hadn't thought of it like that. Is there anything I can do to help?

script.speaker: Parker
script.text: A few small things. Agree on a timetable, so he knows when the study time starts and ends. Keep the phone in another room during lessons. And ask him to show you what he has done at the end of the day, not as a test, just out of interest.

script.speaker: Nguyen
script.text: That sounds reasonable. I'll talk to him tonight.

script.speaker: Parker
script.text: Good. And if you like, I'll send you a short weekly email so you can see how he's getting on without having to ask him.

parts.title: Part 3 · Interview with a student
parts.intro: You will hear a presenter, Hoa, interviewing a university student, Daniel, about studying online.

script.speaker: Hoa
script.text: Daniel, you're in your second year of a degree that's taught almost entirely online. Why did you choose that?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Mainly because of where I live. The nearest university is about three hours away by train, and I couldn't afford the rent in the city. Studying online lets me live with my parents and work part-time.

script.speaker: Hoa
script.text: So it's a practical decision rather than a preference?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: To start with, yes. But I've come to like some things about it. I can watch lectures twice if I don't follow something, and I can pause and take notes without feeling that everyone's waiting for me.

script.speaker: Hoa
script.text: Is there a downside?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Definitely. Loneliness. In the first term I went a whole week without talking to anyone except my family. You miss the small conversations that happen before and after a lecture, where you find out what the others are thinking.

script.speaker: Hoa
script.text: How did you deal with that?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: I set up a study group with three classmates. We meet on a video call every Thursday evening and just talk through the week's reading. It sounds simple, but it has made an enormous difference, both to my marks and my mood.

script.speaker: Hoa
script.text: Would you recommend online study to a school leaver?

script.speaker: Daniel
script.text: Only to someone who's well organised. If you need a teacher to push you, I think it would be difficult. Personally, I'd like to spend the final year on campus, just for the atmosphere.

parts.title: Part 4 · Lecture: Learning well at home
parts.intro: You will hear a lecturer, Dr Anna Lee, giving advice about studying online.

script.speaker: Lee
script.text: Today I'd like to share four strategies that research suggests can improve your learning when you study remotely.

script.speaker: Lee
script.text: The first is to create a boundary between study and the rest of your life. If you can, use one particular place only for work. Even if it's just a corner of the kitchen table, your brain learns that this place means concentration.

script.speaker: Lee
script.text: The second is to work in short, focused sessions. Most people can concentrate hard for about twenty-five or thirty minutes, so rather than spending four hours looking at a screen, study for half an hour and then stand up and move for five minutes.

script.speaker: Lee
script.text: The third strategy may surprise you: don't take notes on everything. Students who copy down every word of a lecture often remember less than those who write only the key ideas in their own words, because summarising forces you to think.

script.speaker: Lee
script.text: The fourth is to test yourself. Instead of rereading a chapter, close the book and try to write down what you remember. It's more uncomfortable, but it is far more effective than simply reading something again.

script.speaker: Lee
script.text: Of course, technology can help or hinder. Some students find that turning off notifications gives them an extra hour a day. Others use an app that blocks social media. The tool matters less than the decision to use one.

script.speaker: Lee
script.text: In the next session, we'll look at how to manage group projects across different time zones. Please read the short article on the course page before then.

questions.text: What did the report say about equipment?
options: Differences in equipment mattered a lot.
Every family had a fast connection and a laptop.
Schools provided all of the equipment needed.
questions.explanation: Some families had a fast connection, others shared one old laptop, and this gap mattered a great deal.

evidence.quote: this gap in equipment mattered a great deal

questions.text: Why did younger children lose the most?
options: They found it hard to concentrate without a teacher.
They had no computers or fast connection at home.
They were too anxious in a crowded classroom.
questions.explanation: Without a teacher in the room, they found it difficult to concentrate and fell behind in reading.

evidence.quote: they found it difficult to concentrate

questions.text: What did many older students like about remote learning?
options: Working at their own speed
Meeting their friends more often online
Having more homework to do each night
questions.explanation: Many said they liked working at their own speed.

evidence.quote: work at their own speed

questions.text: What is the report's overall conclusion?
options: Online learning is bad and should be stopped
It works best with some face-to-face contact
Recorded videos work better than live lessons
questions.explanation: It says online learning works best when combined with face-to-face contact.

evidence.quote: it works best when it is combined with face-to-face contact

questions.text: What do the authors think about teacher training?
options: It is unnecessary because platforms are easy to use
It is too expensive for most schools to offer
It matters, because online teaching is a skill.
questions.explanation: They stress that designing an interesting online lesson takes time to learn.

evidence.quote: teachers need training

options: To complain about the amount of homework set
To ask if online lessons work for his son
To ask the school for a laptop for his son
questions.explanation: He is not sure that Minh's online lessons are working.

evidence.quote: I'm not sure it's working

His results are good.
He is the weakest student in the class

The lessons are too short.

Buy Minh a new phone with fewer apps
Move Minh to another school nearby

Still very worried about his son's phone
Reassured and willing to act

questions.text: Why did Daniel choose to study online?
options: He dislikes lectures and prefers working alone
He wants to travel while he studies abroad
He lives far from the nearest university.
questions.explanation: The university is three hours away and he could not afford the city rent.

questions.text: What does Daniel like about online study?
options: Being able to watch a lecture twice
Having a free laptop from the university
Never having to write notes or essays

Loneliness

He moved to the city to be near classmates
He changed courses to a campus programme
